opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Subject-verb agreement is a nice test case precisely because it forces you to take a position on what the representation of a sentence actually is. On the surface, a sentence is just a sequence of words, so the simplest hypothesis would be that the verb agrees with whatever noun is closest to it. That works most of the time in English, because the subject is usually right before the verb.

But it breaks down in sentences like "The keys to the cabinet are on the table." The noun closest to the verb is "cabinet," which is singular, but the verb is plural because it agrees with "keys." The intervening noun is buried inside a prepositional phrase that modifies the subject, so it's not in the structural position that governs agreement. The rule linguists would write says the verb agrees with the head of the subject noun phrase, and you can only state that rule if you have some notion of hierarchical structure: constituents nested inside other constituents. Linear order alone doesn't give you the right generalization.

That's what made agreement attractive when we started looking at neural networks, in the 2016 paper with Emmanuel Dupoux and Yoav Goldberg. An LSTM doesn't have any explicit tree structure built in. It reads words one at a time. So the question was whether it would learn something functionally equivalent to the hierarchical rule, or whether it would fall back on heuristics like "agree with the most recent noun." The cases that distinguish those hypotheses are the ones with "attractors," intervening nouns that mismatch the subject in number, like "cabinet" in my example. If the model has only learned a linear heuristic, it should fail systematically on those.

We found the models did reasonably well overall but made more errors as the number of attractors increased. Later work, like Gulordava and colleagues and then Marvin and myself, pushed this into harder constructions, such as agreement across relative clauses. Models are often good on the easy cases and much shakier on the structurally complex ones.

I want to be careful about how I interpret this, though. I don't think hierarchical structure has to be explicitly represented as a tree in the system for it to explain behavior. The claim is more that the correct generalization is defined over structure, so any system that generalizes correctly, a human or a network, has to be tracking something that corresponds to that structure. Then the empirical question is whether a given learner, from a given amount of data, actually arrives at that generalization or at a shortcut that happens to work on most of the training distribution.

Humans are also an interesting comparison, because they make attraction errors too. People sometimes say "the key to the cabinets are..." So the human system isn't a flawless tree-processing machine either. Part of what I find interesting is comparing the error patterns. When models and humans fail in similar places, that tells you something. When models fail in places where humans are robust, that suggests the model is missing an inductive bias that humans bring to language acquisition. That connects to the broader question of how much structure needs to be built in versus learned from data, and that's ultimately what I care about.

r001.rationale: It describes hierarchical structure as constituents nested inside other constituents.

r002.rationale: It explains that the verb agrees with the head of the subject noun phrase, even when a closer intervening noun has a different number.

r003.rationale: It says sentences arrive as word sequences, LSTMs have no explicit tree structure, and asks whether they learn a hierarchy equivalent to the structural rule.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the starting point is a very old observation in linguistics: when a verb agrees with its subject, it's not agreeing with whatever noun happens to be closest to it in the string. It's agreeing with the head of the subject phrase, which is a structural notion. Take "the keys to the cabinet are on the table." The noun right before the verb is "cabinet," which is singular, but the verb is plural because it agrees with "keys." If you only had a linear representation of the sentence, "cabinet" would be the obvious candidate. The fact that speakers reliably go with "keys" tells you that whatever mechanism is computing agreement is sensitive to constituency, to the fact that "to the cabinet" is embedded inside the noun phrase headed by "keys."

So hierarchical structure, in that sense, is the explanation for why the pattern is what it is. It's not a stipulation you add on top. If you assume sentences are organized into nested phrases, and that agreement is a relation between a verb and the phrase it's predicated of, the facts just fall out, including facts about long-distance dependencies where a lot of material intervenes between the subject and the verb.

Now, there's an interesting wrinkle, which is that humans aren't perfect at this. People make agreement attraction errors; they'll say "the keys to the cabinet is" at a measurable rate, and the rate goes up when the intervening noun mismatches in number. So the psycholinguistic question is: what does that tell you about the representation? One reading is that the grammar is fully hierarchical but the processing system is noisy, so sometimes a feature from the wrong noun leaks in. That's roughly the cue-based retrieval story. Another reading, the one that gets you into trouble, is that maybe the system isn't fully hierarchical at all and just has strong heuristics that happen to approximate hierarchy most of the time. I don't think that second view is right for humans, because the error patterns are too structured. For instance, attraction is much weaker when the attractor is in a relative clause versus a prepositional phrase, and that's a structural distinction.

And that's exactly what made agreement so appealing to me as a test case for neural language models. These models get trained on sequences of words with no explicit tree structure, so the question is whether they end up inducing something hierarchical anyway. The agreement task gives you a clean diagnostic, because you can construct cases where the linear heuristic and the hierarchical rule give different answers, and see which one the model follows. What we found, going back to the early LSTM work, is a mixed picture. The models do get many of these cases right, more than you'd expect from a pure bag of words, but they also fail in ways that look a lot like the linear heuristic, especially as you push the attractor configurations further from the training distribution. And more recent transformer models are better, but they still have failure modes that suggest the hierarchical generalization isn't quite the thing they've learned. They've learned something that correlates with it.

So I'd say hierarchical structure plays two roles for me. One is explanatory: it's the simplest account of why the agreement pattern in natural language looks the way it does, and why the human errors have the shape they have. The other is methodological: it gives you a precise hypothesis that you can falsify, both in people and in models, which is a lot more useful than asking vaguely whether a system "understands syntax."

r001.rationale: Describes sentences as nested phrases and identifies constituency as a structural property.

r002.rationale: Explains that agreement follows the subject head (“keys”), even when a different-number noun (“cabinet”) is closer to the verb.

r003.rationale: Says language models receive word sequences without explicit tree structure and asks whether they induce hierarchy from them.

astra-6.text:
Subject-verb agreement is a useful case because it lets us distinguish a structural generalization from a simple linear one. If you say, “The key to the cabinets is on the table,” the verb agrees with “key,” even though “cabinets” is closer to it. So the rule isn’t just “make the verb agree with the most recent noun.” You need to identify the head of the subject, and hierarchical sentence structure gives you a way to characterize that relationship.

But I think it’s important to separate that description of the rule from the question of how a speaker—or a neural network—actually produces the right verb. Getting this sentence right doesn’t, by itself, show that a model represents an explicit syntactic tree. There might be other cues that lead it to the same answer. What makes agreement interesting experimentally is that you can construct cases where those cues come apart and ask which generalization the system follows.

Humans also sometimes make agreement errors when there’s an intervening plural noun. That doesn’t mean their grammar is simply linear; it means that implementing a structural dependency involves a processing system that can be subject to interference. So agreement gives us a way to study both the structural knowledge and the mechanisms that make use of it.

r001.rationale: It refers to hierarchical sentence structure and identifying the subject’s head, but does not describe the hierarchy as nested word groups or constituents.

r002.rationale: The “key to the cabinets” example says the verb agrees with “key” even though “cabinets” is closer, tying agreement to the subject’s head.

r003.rationale: It discusses using structure to characterize the relationship, but does not state that structure must be inferred from the word sequence because the sequence does not explicitly represent it.

sol-6.1.text:
Subject-verb agreement is a useful case because it lets us distinguish a structural generalization from a simple linear one. In English, we say “The key to the cabinets is on the table.” The verb agrees with “key,” even though “cabinets” is closer to it. So knowing which noun is closest isn’t enough. You need to identify the head of the subject, and that’s a hierarchical relationship.

But there are two questions here that we should separate. One is how we describe the grammatical rule, and hierarchy gives us a very natural description. The other is what representations and computations people—or neural networks—actually use to produce that behavior. Getting agreement right on ordinary sentences doesn’t by itself establish that a model has learned hierarchical structure, because other cues can often give you the right answer.

That’s why the interesting experiments are ones where those cues come apart: where the structurally correct subject and a nearby noun have different numbers, for example. And even there, we want to look at patterns across constructions and at the errors. Humans sometimes make agreement errors too. The question is how a system tracks the structural relationship, and under what conditions competing information interferes with it.

r001.rationale: The response refers to a hierarchical relationship and the subject’s head, but does not describe sentence structure as nested word groups or constituents.

r002.rationale: The key/cabinets example explicitly says the verb agrees with the structurally relevant subject, “key,” even though “cabinets” is closer.

r003.rationale: The response says proximity alone is insufficient and the subject’s head must be identified, but does not state that syntactic structure is inferred from the word sequence because it is not explicitly represented there.
